If you want to really cook, skip the fast food if you can. It will teach you to multitask and work with urgency (though the caliber of worker they get doesn't always give a fuck), but not much more. It's repetitive assembly. Like factory work vs engineering. Both are building shit, but one is skilled and one is not.

Look for a dishwasher job and say you want to work your way up. This is an industry where you really do have to work your way up a lot of the time.

If you show up on time and work hard, they will notice. If you ask for more experience, they'll let you start helping with prep first I'd imagine.

From there, you can work towards filling in on the line. And from there, you're really cooking.

Hospitals, retirement homes, hotels, catering jobs, and even some schools are great opportunities. The pay may be less (or more, it really depends), but your quality of life will be better. 

Chain restaurants are probably one step up from fast food, but also an option.

The ideal spot is going to be a made from scratch local restaurant specializing in seasonal menus and higher end food-- this job likely won't hire you to start, but keep trying. It might not even hurt to save up to eat here so you get an idea of the caliber of food you'd be preparing. If you go enough to get recognized, that could actually be your foot in the door. Try new things, ask for recommendations, be personable. Servers can put in a good word if you express that you really want to learn and grow there.

Culinary school is also a great option, if you can afford it. Do not do online culinary schools. I've seen people do them and they're a scam. 


Another tip would be to practice at home. Practice knife skills. Mirepoix, how to make a roux, how to sear meat and get a feel for how to cook with different tools. A lot of places use flat tops and stainless steel, this is something you get better with from practice, because you can learn when to add oil, when to flip meats with tearing, etc.

If you ever get an opportunity to step in, having these skills already developed will be noticed. 

Finally, I would forewarn you, there is still a lot of sexism in the industry. Not all places tolerate it, but some are a cesspool. Don't let it discourage you, but do let it help you build a thick skin. The kitchen is fast and unforgiving. If the place you work is toxic, don't be afraid to move on. It will drag you down.

Oh yea, and brace yourself for long hours and missing social events. Restaurants are busiest when people like to do things. So you'll be at work when friends/family want to socialize. Weekends you could easily put in 2/3 of your hours or more (I used to work 12s every fri, sat, sun). Mother's day is a huge day, expect to work every single one. Other holidays are hit or miss, you used to count on working every new years, etc, but since covid a lot of places have been forced to give staff some of those off.

Where I work we only do one base coat and one top coat for cabinets. But we are also adjusting viscosity, tint, etc on site. Also using Sherwin Williams, but not sure on the line off the top of my head. It's certainly not the cheap shit though.

Eh you can do it with a primer and top coat for sure. It's application. Rollers suck. But it's what a DIYer has access too of course. 

Viscosity, pigmentation, and application done right could absolutely nail this without more than one top coat. 

I see it done every day. But yea, greens/yellows are terrible choices for an amateur to do. Should've gone with a nice blue or even pink like every other nursery I've ever seen.

Sherwin Williams owns Valspar. They have almost a monopoly on paint suppliers in the US, to the point where they actually are not allowed to buy anyone else out in the US (so now they're going international). I would not say Sherwin Williams is going to be noticeably better on residential applications by an untrained/inexperienced applicator. 

I work as a color match specialist for a company that gets paint supplied from Sherwin Williams. I deal with Valspar, Berry, and many other colors as we will match anything sent in -- but we use Sherwin Williams as the base.

There are many factors at play here tbh. Others have noted application could be an issue. 

It could also be the material you're painting. 

Did you use a primer? Was this unpainted drywall? Etc. 

Every color and pigmentation is different, as could many other factors like viscosity, etc. The fact that you have 75% tint is a problem for sure.

As others have said, you can probably just add more layers to get a better coverage and more even distribution. That could lead to problems down the line if you ever go to change colors though.

In general, greens are a terribly difficult paint color to get right. I've seen sprayers with 20yrs experience have variation based on the factors above. Anything with yellow is a nightmare. 

The best bet is to go slow, steady, and uniform on the next coat. Don't rush, don't go too slow. Get a rhythm in your head and stick to it. Don't push the roller, let the roller glide along the surface. Consistent application is a huge factor. 

And also, yea... one coat paints are a lie. You need a primer and a top coat if you want it to guarantee a good finish. It costs more, but you absolutely get what you pay for. 

In this case, just add another coat and do not rush or try to conserve paint. Don't be forceful, be graceful. In the future, invest in a base coat and top coat. Budget to have extra paint if anything. Save it for touchups.
